questions.stem: Why is the electrolysis of aqueous solutions more complex than that of molten compounds?

options.text: Because aqueous solutions are always more concentrated
Because water provides additional H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, giving more possible products at the electrodes
Because the electrodes dissolve in water
Because aqueous solutions do not conduct electricity

questions.explanation: In aqueous solutions, water molecules partially dissociate into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. These compete with the ions from the dissolved compound at the electrodes, so there are more possible products to consider.

questions.stem: At the cathode during aqueous electrolysis, what determines whether the metal or hydrogen is produced?

options.text: The reactivity of the metal: if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen is produced instead
The concentration of the solution has no effect

questions.explanation: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (above hydrogen in the reactivity series), hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode instead of the metal. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.

questions.stem: What is produced at the anode during the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution (brine)?
questions.explanation: When a halide ion (like chloride) is present in the solution, the halogen is produced at the anode instead of oxygen. So chlorine gas is produced at the anode during the electrolysis of brine.

questions.stem: What are the three products of the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution (brine)?

options.text: Hydrogen, chlorine, and sodium hydroxide solution

questions.explanation: The electrolysis of brine produces hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide solution remains in the electrolyte. All three products are commercially valuable.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution with inert electrodes, what forms at the cathode?
questions.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are preferentially discharged at the cathode. Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons and are deposited as copper metal: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

questions.stem: At the anode, if the solution does not contain a halide ion, what gas is usually produced?
questions.explanation: If no halide ions are present in the solution, hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from water are discharged at the anode instead, producing oxygen gas: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid, what are the products at the cathode and anode?

options.text: Sulfur at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and sulfur at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode

questions.explanation: In dilute sulfuric acid, H⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode to produce hydrogen gas, and OH⁻ ions are discharged at the anode to produce oxygen gas. The sulfate ions remain in solution. Effectively, the water is decomposed.
